Introduction
The Petitioner, Wanigasuriya Arachchige Charunda Prasad, has invoked the writ jurisdiction
of this Court under Article 140 of the Constitution, seeking, inter alia, writs of certiorari and
mandamus in respect of the refusal of the Consumer Affairs Authority (hereinafter referred to
as the CAA), the 1st Respondent, to pay salary and other emoluments withheld during the
period of his compulsory leave and interdiction, and its failure to grant annual salary
increments.
The application arises from the Petitioner’s employment with the CAA, his arrest and
interdiction following allegations of bribery, his subsequent acquittal by the High Court of
Colombo, and his reinstatement to service.
The principal question for determination is whether the Respondents were entitled to continue
withholding the Petitioner’s salary after his acquittal and reinstatement, despite the absence
of a concluded disciplinary inquiry and the Hon. Attorney-General’s advice recommending
payment of salary arrears.
The application also raises questions concerning the Petitioner’s entitlement to annual salary
increments, the effect of his subsequent resignation, and the circumstances in which this
Court may exercise its discretionary writ jurisdiction to grant the relief sought.
Factual Background
The Petitioner joined the CAA as an Investigation Officer with effect from 01st January 2009.
His letter of appointment dated 23rd December 2008 has been produced, marked P1.
On 01st September 2016, while serving at the Gampaha District Office of the CAA, the
Petitioner and three other officers were arrested by officers of the Commission to Investigate
Allegations of Bribery or Corruption in connection with allegations of soliciting and
accepting a bribe of Rs. 125,000.
Following their arrest, they were produced before the Chief Magistrate’s Court in
proceedings bearing Case No. B 59432/1/2016 and remanded.
Consequent to his arrest and remand, the Petitioner was placed on compulsory leave with
effect from 01st September 2016 under Paragraph 27:7 of Chapter XLVIII of the
Establishments Code, Volume II. The letter dated 09th September 2016 communicating this
decision has been produced, marked P2.
Thereafter, by letter dated 03rd October 2016, marked P3, the Petitioner was informed that the
Board of Directors of the CAA, at its meeting held on 30th September 2016, had decided to
take action under Paragraphs 27:9 and 31:1:10 of Chapter XLVIII of the Establishments
Code. The letter also communicated the Board’s decision to initiate disciplinary action
against him.
Subsequently, an indictment containing eleven charges relating to allegations of soliciting and
accepting bribery was filed against the Petitioner and the other accused before the High Court
of Colombo in Case No. HCB 94/2021. The indictment dated 02nd March 2021 has been
produced, marked P4.
On 18th May 2023, the learned High Court Judge of Colombo, acting under Section 200(1) of
the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, acquitted the Petitioner and the other accused of all
charges without calling defence. A copy of the judgement has been produced and marked as
Following his acquittal, the Petitioner made representations seeking reinstatement in service.
By letter dated 28th July 2023, marked P6, the Petitioner was informed that the Board of
Directors, at its meeting held on 28th June 2023, had decided to reinstate him in service with
effect from 01st August 2023.
The Petitioner was initially attached to the Monaragala District Office. Subsequently,
following an appeal made to the 2nd Respondent, he was transferred to the Head Office with
effect from 23rd November 2023. The relevant letter has been produced and marked as P7.
The Petitioner continued in service until his resignation on 24th July 2024. He states that his
resignation was necessitated by his mother’s illness. His resignation letter has been produced
and marked as P8.
The Petitioner states that, notwithstanding his acquittal and subsequent reinstatement, the
CAA failed to pay the salary and other emoluments withheld during the period commencing
on 01st September 2016 and ending upon his reinstatement.
He further complains that the CAA did not grant annual salary increments for the period
commencing on 01st September 2016 and ending on 24th July 2024.
The Petitioner also maintains that his gratuity should be calculated after taking into account
the salary increments to which he claims entitlement.
The Petitioner refers to a complaint made by another officer involved in the same incident,
namely Nambukara Appu Kapuge Harshana Kumara, to the Commissioner-General of
Labour on 06th September 2023.
The documents related to that complaint have been produced and marked as P9(a) to P9(c).
Of particular significance is the letter dated 17th October 2023, marked P9(b), addressed by
the Chairman of the CAA to the Labour Officer, Colombo South.
In that letter, the Chairman stated that the officers, including the Petitioner concerned, had not
performed their duties from 01st September 2016 to 31st July 2023 and that the CAA therefore
decided not to pay remuneration for that period. For ease of reference, attention is drawn to
paragraph 7 of the letter marked P9(b).
“7.ඉහත මහාධිකරණ නඩු තීන්දුව අධිකාරිය විසින් කිසිදු ආකාරයකින් අභිය ෝගයට ලක්
න ොකරන අතර, ඔවුන්ව වැඩ තහනමට ලක්ව සිටි 2016.09.01 දින සිට 2023.07.31 දින
දක්වා කාලය සඳහා ඔවුන් ස ේවයට පැමිණ වැටුප් උපයා ගැනීම සිදුකර න ොමැති බැවින්ද,
එම කාලයට අදාළව වැටුප් වර්ධක උපයා ගෙන න ොමැති බැවින් ද එම ස ේවය න ොකල
කාලය සඳහා වැටුප් න ොගෙවීමට අධිකාරිය ගෙන තිබූ තීරණය සම්බන්ධයෙන් නීතිපති
දෙපාර්තමේන්තුව වෙත අධිකාරියේ සභාපති ශ්‍රේෂ්ඨාධිකරණයේ නීතිඥ ශාන්ත නිරිඇල්ල
මහතා විසින් නීතිමය උපදෙස් ලබාගැනීමට ය ොමුකර ඇති අතර නීතිපති උපදෙස් අනුව ඉදිරි
කටයුතු සිදු කරනු ඇත. එම ලිපියේ පිටපතක් මේ සමඟ අමුණා ඇත (ඇමුණුම 03).”
The letter further stated that the CAA had sought advice from the Hon. Attorney-General on
the matter.
The Petitioner also refers to a complaint made by the said officer to the Human Rights
Commission of Sri Lanka, bearing No. HRC/HO/3532/23, marked P10.
The Attorney-General’s advice dated 06th December 2024 has been produced by the
Respondents, marked R1.
According to R1, the Hon. Attorney-General advised that, since the High Court acquitted the
Petitioner, the Disciplinary Authority reinstated him in service, and no appeal had been
preferred against the acquittal, arrears of salary should be paid for the period from 01st
September 2016 to 01st August 2023. Attention is drawn to the last paragraph of the letter
marked R1.
“ඒ අනුව අදාල නිලධාරීන් අංක HCB/94/2021 දරන මහාධිකරණ නඩු තීන්දුවෙන් නිද ොස්
ක ොට නිදහස් කිරීම, එකී නඩු තීන්දුවට එරෙහිව අභියාචනයක් න ොකිරීමට සහ විනය
බලධරයා එකී නිලධාරීන් නැවත ස ේවයේ පිහිටිවීමට දැනටමත් කටයුතු කිරීම යන කරුණ
මත 2016.09.01 දින සිට 2023.08.01 දින දක්වා හිඟ වැටුප් ගෙවිය යුතු බවට මාගේ මතය
The Petitioner further states that, at a meeting held on 26th December 2024, the 3rd
Respondent informed the officers concerned that the Attorney-General’s advice had been
submitted to the Board of Directors and that the Board had decided to conduct a preliminary
inquiry concerning the incident.
According to the Petitioner, although the CAA communicated its intention to initiate
disciplinary proceedings as far back as October 2016, it did not conclude any disciplinary
inquiry before his resignation in July 2024.
The Petitioner also relies upon the letter dated 06th July 2020, marked P12, alleging that the
CAA had adopted a different approach in comparable circumstances.
By letter dated 07th January 2025, marked P11, the Petitioner and other officers again
requested the CAA to resolve their grievances.
The Petitioner complains that no satisfactory response was received.
In these circumstances, he seeks writs of certiorari to quash the decisions refusing payment
of withheld remuneration and annual salary increments, and writs of mandamus directing
payment of salary arrears, the grant of increments, and the consequential calculation of
gratuity.
Position of the Respondents
The Respondents resist the application. Their principal contention is that the Petitioner’s
acquittal in criminal proceedings does not automatically entitle him to payment of the salary
and other emoluments withheld during interdiction.
It is submitted that criminal proceedings and departmental disciplinary proceedings are
distinct and that an acquittal by a criminal court does not necessarily amount to exoneration
for disciplinary purposes.
The Respondents further maintain that the Petitioner did not perform duties during the period
of compulsory leave and interdiction and was therefore not entitled to remuneration for that
period.
It is also contended that annual salary increments are not automatic entitlements but are
subject to the applicable conditions of service.
The Respondents raise a preliminary objection that the Petitioner has failed to identify with
sufficient certainty the administrative decisions sought to be quashed by writs of certiorari.
They further submit that the Petitioner has failed to establish a clear legal right and a
corresponding public duty sufficient to justify the issuance of writs of mandamus.
Issues for Determination
Having considered the pleadings, documents and submissions, the principal issues to be
determined are;
• whether the decisions sought to be quashed have been sufficiently identified;
• whether the Petitioner’s acquittal and reinstatement confer an entitlement to the
withheld salary;
• whether the failure to conclude disciplinary proceedings affects the legality of the
continued non-payment; and what significance should be attached to the Attorney-
General’s advice, marked R1.
It is also necessary to determine whether the Petitioner is entitled to annual salary increments,
whether his subsequent resignation affects any accrued financial rights, and whether the
circumstances justify the issuance of the writs sought.
Preliminary Objection
Learned State Counsel submits that the application is not maintainable because the Petitioner
has failed to identify the administrative decisions sought to be quashed.
It is contended that prayers (e) and (f) refer generally to decisions refusing payment of back
wages and annual salary increments without identifying the dates of those decisions or the
persons responsible for making them.
Ordinarily, a writ of certiorari is directed against an identifiable administrative decision. The
Court must be able to identify the challenged decision and the grounds on which its validity is
questioned.
However, the absence of a formal decision addressed directly to an applicant does not
necessarily establish that no administrative decision was made.
In the present application, P9(b) expressly records that the CAA had decided not to pay
remuneration for the relevant period because the officers concerned had not performed duties.
Although P9(b) was addressed to the Labour Officer in connection with another officer’s
complaint, it discloses the position adopted by the CAA concerning the financial claims
arising from the same incident.
The Petitioner has also specifically complained of the continued refusal to pay his salary and
grant annual increments.
Furthermore, the Respondents have produced the Attorney-General’s advice marked R1,
which directly concerns the question of payment of salary arrears.
In these circumstances, I cannot accept the contention that the application must fail merely
because the Petitioner has not produced a formal letter addressed to him communicating the
refusal.
The material before this Court sufficiently discloses an administrative position concerning
non-payment which is capable of judicial examination.
Nevertheless, the distinction between the refusal of salary arrears and the alleged refusal of
increments must be maintained, as the evidentiary foundation for the two claims is not
identical.
Accordingly, I reject the preliminary objection insofar as it seeks to dismiss the entire
application without considering the merits.
The Relevant Provisions of the Establishments Code
The letters marked P2 and P3 expressly refer to Chapter XLVIII of the Establishments Code.
The Respondents have also relied upon the provisions of that Chapter in justifying the
decisions concerning the Petitioner.
It is therefore necessary to examine the relevant provisions, while recognising that the CAA
is a statutory authority and that the precise applicability of the Establishments Code must be
determined in the light of the governing conditions of service.
Paragraph 31:10 provides that the non-payment of emoluments or payment of one-half of the
emoluments of an officer under interdiction is to be decided by the Disciplinary Authority.
Paragraph 31:11 identifies circumstances in which an interdicted officer should not receive
emoluments during interdiction.
Paragraph 31:11:1 specifically refers to circumstances where legal proceedings have been
initiated for an offence of bribery or corruption.
The allegations against the Petitioner concerned bribery. Accordingly, if these provisions
apply, the initial withholding of emoluments during interdiction cannot be regarded as
unlawful merely because the Petitioner was subsequently acquitted.
However, the authority to withhold emoluments during interdiction must be distinguished
from the ultimate determination of whether those emoluments should remain unpaid after the
conclusion of the relevant proceedings.
Paragraph 31:14 provides that where a formal disciplinary inquiry results in the imposition of
a punishment less than dismissal, the Disciplinary Authority should decide whether the full
emoluments withheld, or a percentage thereof, should be paid. Such determination forms part
of the disciplinary order.
Paragraph 31:15 defines the expression “emoluments” by reference to the emoluments of the
officer’s substantive post. It excludes allowances in the nature of duty allowances and
reimbursements of expenditure incurred in the performance of official duties, including
travel, transport, and combined allowances.
Paragraph 31:17 recognises that reinstatement of an officer who has not been found guilty,
following interdiction without sufficient cause, may result in payment of emoluments for a
period during which no work was performed. The provision therefore requires the appropriate
authority to satisfy itself before interdicting an officer.
These provisions demonstrate that the initial withholding of emoluments and their ultimate
payment are distinct matters.
Paragraph 31:11:1 cannot, by itself, be interpreted as authorising the permanent forfeiture of
salary following acquittal and reinstatement, irrespective of the subsequent conduct of the
Disciplinary Authority.
Equally, Paragraph 31:17 does not establish that every criminal acquittal automatically
entitles an officer to full back wages.
The ultimate entitlement must be determined upon the applicable legal provisions and the
particular circumstances of the case.
Effect of Criminal Acquittal and Reinstatement
The High Court acquitted the Petitioner on 18th May 2023 under Section 200(1) of the Code
of Criminal Procedure Act, without calling the defence. That acquittal ended the criminal
proceedings. Nevertheless, an acquittal in criminal proceedings does not necessarily prevent a
disciplinary authority from conducting an independent inquiry into the same conduct.
The purposes and standards of proof applicable to criminal and disciplinary proceedings are
different. Therefore, I do not accept the proposition that the Petitioner’s criminal acquittal,
considered in isolation, automatically entitled him to recover the entirety of the salary
withheld during interdiction.
However, the present case does not concern criminal acquittal alone. The CAA subsequently
decided to reinstate the Petitioner with effect from 01st August 2023. There is no material
establishing that the reinstatement was made subject to a concluded finding of a disciplinary
action or that the CAA had imposed any disciplinary order upon the Petitioner. More
importantly, this Court has not been presented with any concluded disciplinary inquiry or
final disciplinary order.
The legal effect of these circumstances must therefore be examined together, not separately.
The Decision in Nandadasa v M.S. Jayasinghe
In Nandadasa v. M. S. Jayasinghe, Secretary, Ministry of Justice and Constitutional
Affairs and Others (2001) 1 SLR 14, the Supreme Court considered the legality of a
disciplinary authority’s decision to withhold permanently the salary of a public officer who
had been interdicted following allegations of bribery.
The petitioner in that case was prosecuted for bribery and subsequently acquitted. Following
his acquittal, he was reinstated subject to a disciplinary inquiry. The inquiring officer
exonerated him of all charges. However, the disciplinary authority rejected those findings,
found him guilty and directed that the salary withheld during interdiction should not be paid.
The only other punishment imposed was a warning.
Justice Mark Fernando, examining the relevant provisions of Chapter XLVIII of the
Establishments Code, drew a distinction between withholding salary during interdiction and
subsequently deciding that the withheld salary should not be paid.
Justice Fernando observed at page 24 as:
“The initial withholding of salary during interdiction is not a punishment. It cannot
be a punishment, because it is an order made before there is any finding of guilt.”
The Supreme Court then examined whether the subsequent non-payment could lawfully be
imposed independently of a disciplinary punishment.
Under the provisions then applicable, the Court held that the order concerning withheld salary
was a consequence of punishment and that, since the disciplinary authority had imposed only
a warning, which was expressly excluded from the category of punishments, the order
directing non-payment lacked the necessary legal foundation. The Supreme Court also found
serious violations of natural justice in the manner in which the disciplinary authority rejected
the inquiring officer’s findings and in the subsequent consideration of the petitioner’s appeal.
The Supreme Court quashed the impugned orders and held the petitioner entitled to the salary
withheld during interdiction, together with interest.
The importance of the reasoning of Nandadasa lies in the distinction between provisional
withholding of emoluments during interdiction and their ultimate deprivation.
The former does not necessarily establish the legality of the latter. However, a factual
distinction exists between the Nandadasa judgement and the present application.
In Nandadasa, a disciplinary inquiry had been conducted and a final disciplinary order made,
although that order was subsequently found to be unlawful.
In the present application, no concluded disciplinary inquiry or final disciplinary order has
been established.
Nevertheless, the underlying principle remains relevant. The ultimate refusal to pay withheld
emoluments must be supported by the applicable legal provisions and cannot be justified
solely by reference to the original interdiction.
The Supreme Court also emphasised the importance of disclosing findings and reasons to an
officer affected by an adverse disciplinary decision.
The Decision in Don Karunasena Athukorala
In Don Karunasena Athukorala v. H. M. Gunasekera and Others (2016) 1 Sri LR 286, the
Supreme Court considered the withholding of emoluments during interdiction and the
financial consequences of disciplinary proceedings against a public officer.
The petitioner, a school principal, had been interdicted following allegations of bribery and
was subsequently acquitted in criminal proceedings.
However, an independent disciplinary inquiry was conducted, and he was found guilty of
nine charges of misconduct.
The disciplinary authority thereafter determined that half wages should be paid during the
period of interdiction.
Justice Prasanna Jayawardena, examining the relevant provisions of Chapter XLVIII of the
Establishments Code, upheld the decision concerning payment of half wages.
The Supreme Court also considered the legality of deductions from the petitioner’s pension
and gratuity and set aside the pension deduction because the prescribed procedural
requirements had not been complied with. The decision confirms that criminal acquittal does
not automatically invalidate an earlier interdiction or establish an unconditional entitlement to
full emoluments.
It also demonstrates that the financial consequences of disciplinary proceedings must be
determined in accordance with the applicable legal provisions.
The distinction between that case and the present application is significant.
In Athukorala, disciplinary proceedings had been concluded, and findings of misconduct had
been made.
In the present application, the CAA communicated its intention to initiate disciplinary
proceedings in October 2016 but did not establish that any disciplinary inquiry had been
concluded before the Petitioner’s resignation.
Accordingly, Athukorala supports the Respondents’ contention that criminal acquittal does
not automatically entitle an employee to back wages.
However, it does not resolve the separate question whether the CAA may continue to deny
payment indefinitely without concluding disciplinary proceedings or making a lawful
determination concerning the withheld salary.
The Decision in Rannulu Sugath Mohana Mendis
In Rannulu Sugath Mohana Mendis v. D. K. A. Sanath Kumara and Others,
SC/FR/100/2022, decided on 06th October 2023, the Supreme Court considered the
prolonged interdiction of a police officer without the conduct of a preliminary investigation
as required by the applicable provisions of Chapter XLVIII of the Establishments Code.
The petitioner in that case had been interdicted without pay following his arrest in connection
with alleged criminal offences.
Although the relevant authority possessed the power to interdict him, no preliminary
investigation had been conducted for more than two years.
Justice Thurairaja, examined Paragraphs 31:3, 31:4, 31:5:3, 31:7 and 27:10 of the
Establishments Code and emphasised the duty of the disciplinary authority to comply with
the prescribed procedural requirements.
Of particular relevance is the Supreme Court’s consideration of Paragraph 27:10, as amended
by Public Administration Circular No. 06/2004 dated 15th December 2004.
The provision required a preliminary investigation to be conducted within two months in the
circumstances contemplated therein.
The Supreme Court also considered Paragraph 27:10:1, which permits the disciplinary
authority, in the circumstances specified by that provision, to authorise payment of salary not
exceeding one-half where the criminal proceedings remain unresolved beyond one year.
The Supreme Court strongly criticised the failure to commence a preliminary investigation
even after the lapse of two years.
The petitioner was subsequently reinstated during the pendency of the fundamental rights
application, and arrears of salary were paid.
The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 12(1) and
14(1)(g) of the Constitution were violated.
Significantly, the Court directed the retrospective grant of salary increments, benefits and
promotions, in addition to awarding compensation.
The decision demonstrates that the exercise of disciplinary powers is subject to the
procedural safeguards prescribed by law and that prolonged administrative inaction may have
consequences affecting an officer’s financial entitlements.
It must nevertheless be recognised that Rannulu Sugath Mohana Mendis arose in the
exercise of the Supreme Court’s fundamental rights jurisdiction and concerned facts
materially different from those in the present application.
Furthermore, the applicability of the precise procedural requirements considered in that case
to employees of the CAA depends upon the governing service rules.
Nevertheless, the broader principle is relevant. A disciplinary authority must exercise its
powers within the framework prescribed by law and cannot leave an employee’s disciplinary
position unresolved indefinitely.
Failure to Conduct Disciplinary Proceedings
The Petitioner was informed in October 2016 that the Board of Directors had decided to
initiate disciplinary proceedings against him. The criminal proceedings were concluded on
18th May 2023. Thereafter, the CAA reinstated him in service with effect from 01st August
2023. He continued in service until his resignation on 24th July 2024.
Thus, nearly eight years elapsed between the CAA’s decision to initiate disciplinary action
and the Petitioner’s resignation.
During that period, no concluded disciplinary inquiry or final disciplinary determination has
been established before this Court.
The Respondents have not satisfactorily explained why the proposed disciplinary proceedings
remained unresolved for such a prolonged period.
The failure assumes particular significance because the CAA reinstated the Petitioner
following his acquittal and permitted him to resume his duties.
If the CAA considered that the Petitioner’s conduct nevertheless warranted disciplinary
action, it was incumbent upon the competent authority to address that matter in accordance
with the applicable disciplinary rules.
The CAA cannot rely upon its own failure to conclude disciplinary proceedings as a complete
justification for the permanent deprivation of the Petitioner’s financial benefits.
To accept such a proposition would permit an administrative authority to leave an employee’s
financial position unresolved indefinitely and thereafter rely upon that very uncertainty to
defeat his claim.
Such an approach would be inconsistent with the requirements of fairness and reasonableness
governing the exercise of administrative powers.
The present case is not one in which the CAA concluded a disciplinary inquiry and imposed a
punishment affecting the Petitioner’s entitlement to salary.
Nor has any final disciplinary determination been established declaring that the Petitioner
was guilty of misconduct warranting permanent non-payment of the withheld emoluments.
The prolonged failure to conduct disciplinary proceedings must therefore be considered
together with the acquittal, reinstatement and subsequent advice of the Attorney-General.
The Failure to Communicate Reasons
There is another significant aspect of the CAA’s conduct.
Although the CAA had decided not to pay the withheld remuneration, no reasoned decision
explaining the legal basis for such non-payment appears to have been communicated to the
Petitioner.
The letter marked P9(b), addressed to the Labour Officer in connection with another officer’s
complaint, states that the CAA had decided not to pay remuneration because the officers
concerned had not performed duties during the relevant period. However, that letter was not
addressed to the Petitioner. Nor does it disclose any determination of his entitlement under
the applicable provisions of the Establishments Code. It is particularly significant that the
CAA had reinstated the Petitioner following his acquittal without having concluded
disciplinary proceedings against him. In these circumstances, the CAA was required to
address his claim in accordance with the applicable legal provisions and communicate a
decision supported by lawful reasons.
The failure to communicate such a decision assumes greater significance when considered
alongside the prolonged failure to conduct disciplinary proceedings.
The Petitioner was left without a determination of his disciplinary responsibility and without
an adequate explanation of the legal basis upon which his financial claims were being denied.
An administrative authority cannot merely withhold financial benefits and leave the affected
person to ascertain the reasons for that decision from correspondence addressed to another
institution concerning another employee.
The importance of communicating findings and reasons was emphasised by Fernando J. in
Nandadasa, although the particular statutory context of that case differed from the present
application.
In Rannulu Sugath Mohana Mendis, the Supreme Court likewise emphasised that
administrative decisions must be supported by material capable of justifying them when
challenged before a court.
In the present case, the failure to communicate a reasoned decision is a material consideration
in determining whether the CAA acted lawfully and reasonably.
Legal Effect of the Attorney-General’s Advice Marked R1
A further matter of considerable significance is the advice furnished by the Hon. Attorney-
General dated 06th December 2024, which has been produced by the Respondents marked
According to R1, the Attorney-General advised that, since the Petitioner had been acquitted
by the High Court, the Disciplinary Authority had reinstated him in service, and no appeal
had been preferred against the acquittal, arrears of salary should be paid for the period
commencing on 01st September 2016 and ending on 01st August 2023.
Thus, the precise question concerning the payment of salary withheld during the period of
compulsory leave and interdiction was considered by the Attorney-General.
The advice was not confined to a general observation concerning the Petitioner’s acquittal. It
addressed the financial consequences of the acquittal and reinstatement and identified the
period for which salary arrears should be paid.
It is necessary to emphasise that advice furnished by the Attorney-General does not, by itself,
constitute a binding administrative determination requiring payment.
The responsibility for making the relevant administrative decision remains with the authority
upon which the law confers that power.
Nevertheless, advice furnished by the Attorney-General on a question of law is plainly a
material consideration in determining whether the subsequent conduct of the Authority was
lawful and reasonable.
The CAA was not entitled to disregard that advice arbitrarily.
If the CAA considered that the advice should not be followed, it was incumbent upon the
competent decision-making body to identify a lawful basis for adopting a different position.
In the present application, the Respondents have not demonstrated that a reasoned
determination rejecting the Petitioner’s claim, notwithstanding the advice contained in R1,
was communicated to him.
The explanation appearing in P9(b), namely that the officers concerned had not performed
duties during the relevant period, does not satisfactorily answer the question.
The Petitioner’s absence from service resulted from compulsory leave and interdiction
imposed upon him by the CAA itself.
Moreover, the Establishments Code expressly contemplates circumstances in which
emoluments withheld during interdiction may subsequently become payable.
The mere fact that an officer did not perform duties during interdiction cannot therefore be
treated as an absolute bar to the subsequent payment of withheld salary.
The significance of R1 is further reinforced by the absence of a concluded disciplinary
inquiry or an adverse disciplinary order.
The CAA had decided to initiate disciplinary proceedings in October 2016 but failed to bring
those proceedings to a conclusion before the Petitioner’s resignation.
The Attorney-General’s advice must therefore be considered together with the Petitioner’s
acquittal, reinstatement, the absence of an adverse disciplinary determination and the CAA’s
prolonged failure to conclude disciplinary proceedings.
In these circumstances, I am of the view that the continued refusal to pay the Petitioner’s
salary arrears, without identifying a lawful basis for departing from the advice contained in
R1, cannot be justified merely upon the ground that he did not perform duties during the
period of interdiction.
Effect of the Petitioner’s Resignation
The Respondents have also relied upon the Petitioner’s resignation on 24th July 2024. In my
view, resignation does not, merely by itself, extinguish financial rights which may have
accrued during employment.
The Petitioner’s entitlement to withheld salary and eligible increments must therefore be
determined by reference to the applicable legal provisions and the circumstances giving rise
to those claims. The CAA cannot rely upon the Petitioner’s resignation as an explanation for
its failure to conclude disciplinary proceedings during the preceding years. It is also
significant that the Petitioner continued in service for nearly one year after reinstatement.
During that period, the CAA had the opportunity to take appropriate disciplinary action, if
such action was considered necessary and permissible.
The Petitioner’s subsequent resignation cannot retrospectively justify the prolonged failure to
conduct disciplinary proceedings or the refusal to determine his financial entitlements.
Violation of Principles of Natural Justice
Having regard to the cumulative effect of these circumstances, I am satisfied that the
Petitioner has established the unreasonableness and procedural impropriety of the CAA
warranting judicial intervention regarding the withheld salary of the Petitioner. Further, I am
satisfied that the CAA failed to give reasons for withholding the arrears of salary during the
period of interdiction, which violates the Principles of Natural Justice.
Accordingly, I am of the view that the CAA’s continued refusal to pay the salary arrears
cannot be sustained.
Meaning of Emoluments Under Section 31:15
It is necessary to clarify the scope of the financial entitlement claimed by the Petitioner.
Paragraph 31:15 of Chapter XLVIII defines the expression “emoluments” as the emoluments
attached to an officer’s substantive post. The provision expressly excludes allowances in the
nature of duty allowances and reimbursements of expenditure incurred in the performance of
official duties, including travel, transport and combined allowances.
Accordingly, an entitlement to recover withheld emoluments does not necessarily extend to
allowances payable only upon the actual performance of official duties or the incurring of
expenditure in connection with those duties.
Any amount payable to the Petitioner must therefore be calculated based on the salary and
other emoluments lawfully attached to his substantive post, subject to the exclusions
prescribed by the applicable provisions.
The Petitioner cannot claim reimbursement of expenses which were never incurred merely
because he is entitled to recover salary withheld during interdiction.
Annual Salary Increments
The Petitioner also seeks writs of certiorari and mandamus in respect of annual salary
increments for the period commencing on 01st September 2016 and ending on 24th July 2024.
This claim requires separate consideration.
An annual salary increment is not necessarily an unconditional entitlement arising merely
from the passage of time. Ordinarily, the grant of an increment depends upon the applicable
conditions of service, satisfactory performance and eligibility under the relevant salary
scheme. An employee claiming increments must therefore establish that the conditions
governing their grant have been satisfied.
However, Paragraphs 24:6 and 24:7 of Chapter XLVIII of the Establishments Code make
specific provision concerning salary increments in the context of disciplinary proceedings.
Paragraph 24:6 provides that where deferment, reduction or stoppage of a salary increment is
ordered as part of a disciplinary order, the order should be implemented with reference to the
salary step last received by the officer. The provision further contemplates the grant of
subsequent increments even where the officer was not in service. Paragraph 24:7 provides
that where an order not to pay arrears of salary during interdiction forms part of a disciplinary
order, the officer will not be entitled to arrears of salary increments for which he would
otherwise have been eligible. However, the provision expressly requires that the officer be
placed on the appropriate step of the salary scale, taking into account the increments for
which he would have been eligible, notwithstanding the fact that he was not in service. These
provisions demonstrate that the non-payment of salary arrears during interdiction does not
necessarily justify the permanent denial of salary progression. It is important to distinguish
between the actual payment of arrears of increments and the recognition of eligible
increments for determining the appropriate salary step.
In the present application, no concluded disciplinary inquiry or final disciplinary order
imposing stoppage, deferment or reduction of increments has been established.
The Petitioner was reinstated with effect from 01st August 2023 and thereafter continued in
service until 24th July 2024.
The CAA cannot therefore rely merely upon his absence from service during interdiction as a
sufficient basis for refusing to recognise increments for which he was otherwise eligible.
However, it does not follow that the Petitioner is automatically entitled to every increment
claimed. The Petitioner must establish his eligibility under the applicable service rules. The
position relating to the period following reinstatement is particularly significant. The
Petitioner actually performed duties from 01st August 2023 until his resignation.
If his salary upon reinstatement was fixed at an incorrect step because otherwise eligible
increments had not been recognised, that error may have affected the salary payable during
the subsequent period of actual service. It may also have affected the computation of gratuity
and other terminal benefits.
The decision in Rannulu Sugath Mohana Mendis is relevant in this context.
The Supreme Court directed the retrospective grant of salary increments, benefits and
promotions upon finding that the relevant authorities had violated the petitioner’s
fundamental rights.
Nevertheless, that decision does not dispense with the requirement to establish eligibility
under the governing service rules in every case.
Accordingly, I am of the view that the Petitioner is entitled to have his eligibility for annual
increments determined in accordance with the applicable conditions of service and, where
such eligibility is established, to have those increments recognised for the purpose of
determining his appropriate salary step.
Any consequential arrears arising from an incorrect salary placement following reinstatement
must also be addressed in accordance with law.
Gratuity
The Petitioner also seeks a writ of mandamus directing the Respondents to calculate his
gratuity after granting the annual salary increments to which he claims entitlement.
The claim for gratuity is consequential upon the determination of the Petitioner’s correct
salary.
If the salary payable to him upon reinstatement was incorrectly calculated by reason of the
failure to recognise eligible increments, the appropriate salary for the purpose of computing
gratuity may require reconsideration.
However, the calculation of gratuity must be made in accordance with the applicable
statutory provisions and conditions of service.
Accordingly, any correction of the Petitioner’s salary should be reflected in the calculation of
gratuity to the extent required by law.
PAYE Tax
The Petitioner also seeks a direction that PAYE tax should not be deducted from any lump-
sum payment of salary arrears. I am unable to accept this claim as an unconditional
entitlement. Any salary arrears or other remuneration payable to the Petitioner must be dealt
with in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Inland Revenue Act and the statutory
requirements governing deductions of income tax. The fact that remuneration is paid in a
lump sum following a period of withholding does not, by itself, establish an exemption from
taxation.
Accordingly, any payment made pursuant to this judgement shall be subject to such
deductions as are required by law.
Conclusion
The final question is whether the circumstances of this application justify the issuance of the
writs of certiorari and mandamus sought by the Petitioner. A writ of certiorari is directed
towards quashing an administrative decision which is unlawful or otherwise amenable to
judicial review, whereas a writ of mandamus ordinarily requires the existence of an
enforceable legal right and a corresponding public duty.
The writ jurisdiction cannot be exercised merely because an applicant considers an
administrative decision unfair or because the Court considers that a different decision would
have been preferable.
However, where a public authority fails to discharge a duty imposed by law, acts upon an
irrelevant consideration, or refuses to exercise its powers in accordance with the applicable
legal framework, the Court may intervene.
In the present application, the Petitioner has established circumstances which, considered
cumulatively, justify judicial intervention. The criminal proceedings against him were
concluded by an acquittal. The CAA subsequently reinstated him. No concluded disciplinary
inquiry or adverse disciplinary order has been established. The Attorney-General expressly
advised payment of salary arrears for the relevant period.
The CAA nevertheless continued to refuse payment without communicating a reasoned
determination establishing the legal basis for departing from that advice.
The explanation disclosed in P9(b), namely that the officers concerned did not perform duties
during the period of interdiction, is insufficient by itself to justify permanent non-payment.
The Respondents have not demonstrated a lawful basis for treating the original withholding
of salary as an unconditional and permanent deprivation of the amounts withheld.
In these circumstances, I am satisfied that the continued refusal to pay the Petitioner’s salary
arrears is legally unsustainable.
The decision of the CAA refusing payment of the withheld remuneration, as disclosed in the
letter dated 17th October 2023, marked P9(b), expressly concerns the Petitioner and the other
three officers involved in the same incident. The reason advanced for that decision was that
the officers had not performed duties during the period of interdiction. For the reasons
discussed above, that consideration alone cannot justify the permanent deprivation of the
Petitioner’s withheld remuneration in the circumstances of this case. Furthermore,
notwithstanding the Hon. Attorney-General’s subsequent advice recommending payment, the
CAA continued to maintain its earlier position without demonstrating a lawful basis for doing
so. I am therefore satisfied that the decision disclosed in P9(b), insofar as it relates to the
refusal to pay the Petitioner’s withheld remuneration, is liable to be quashed by a writ of
certiorari.
The claim for annual salary increments stands on a different footing.
The Petitioner has not established an unconditional entitlement to every increment claimed
merely by relying upon his acquittal and reinstatement.
Nevertheless, the CAA must determine his eligibility in accordance with the applicable
service rules and recognise any increments for which he was eligible when fixing his salary
upon reinstatement.
The consequential calculation of gratuity must likewise be made in accordance with law.
Order
For the foregoing reasons, I am of the view that the Petitioner has established sufficient
grounds for the exercise of the discretionary writ jurisdiction of this Court.
Accordingly, the application is allowed in part.
A writ of certiorari is issued quashing the decision of the CAA refusing payment of the
Petitioner’s salary arrears for the period commencing on 01st September 2016 and ending
upon his reinstatement with effect from 01st August 2023, insofar as that refusal is founded
upon the ground that the Petitioner did not perform duties during the relevant period.
A writ of mandamus is issued directing the CAA to calculate and pay the salary arrears
lawfully due to the Petitioner for the said period, having regard to the applicable conditions of
service and the advice of the Hon. Attorney-General dated 06th December 2024, marked R1.
In calculating the amount payable, the Respondents shall distinguish the salary and
emoluments attached to the Petitioner’s substantive post from duty-related allowances and
reimbursements excluded under Paragraph 31:15 of Chapter XLVIII of the Establishments
Code, insofar as that provision governs his employment.
In respect of annual salary increments, the CAA is directed to determine the increments for
which the Petitioner was eligible under the applicable service rules during the period
commencing on 01st September 2016 and ending on 24th July 2024.
In making that determination, the CAA shall distinguish between the payment of arrears of
increments during interdiction and the recognition of eligible increments for the purpose of
determining the appropriate salary step upon reinstatement.
Any increments for which the Petitioner was lawfully eligible shall be recognised in fixing
his salary, and any consequential arrears arising from an incorrect salary placement following
reinstatement shall be calculated and paid in accordance with law.
The Respondents shall also reconsider the computation of the Petitioner’s gratuity and make
any consequential adjustment required by the applicable legal provisions.
The prayer seeking a direction prohibiting PAYE tax deductions is refused. Any payments
made pursuant to this judgement shall remain subject to the applicable tax laws.
The Respondents shall take the necessary steps to give effect to the foregoing directions
within three months from the date of this judgement.
The application is accordingly allowed in part.
Considering all the circumstances of this Application, I make no Order as to costs.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
B. Sasi Mahendran, J
